We know that decisions made in Washington, D.C. have significant consequences for our state and local budgets, our economy, and our communities. Few places feel these impacts more directly than Fairfax County, home to more than 82,000 federal workers and 3,800 contractors.

H.R. 1 brings sweeping changes to federal policy concerning SNAP and Medicaid. It restructures the federal-state-local partnership and marks a major structural change to the cornerstone social safety net programs since their inception. This new law introduces unfunded mandates and cost ships from the federal government directly onto states and localities. It not only imposes significant new administrative burdens and policy requirements, but also restricts access for current and future

beneficiaries. The result will be a fraying of our social safety net, leading to predictable increases in food insecurity and the uninsured within our constituency. The need in our community, however, will not diminish. Our local government's budgets will be forced to develop strategies to replace lost federal support. We anticipate increased demand for locally funded food access services, that more residents will lose coverage, that will lose health insurance coverage, that they might delay necessary medical treatments resulting in higher utilizations of emergency

medical services, such as emergency rooms for primary care, as well as ambulances for transportation to the hospital, and will also likely dramatically increase uncompensated care costs that are going to be borne by our local hospital systems. Specifically talking about the changes to the SNAP program, the change to SNAP administration is a direct hit to our operational budget. The federal share of administrative costs has been cut from 50%

to just 25%. The Virginia Department of Social Services has already indicated and confirmed that this increase or this shifting will move our local match from 15.5% to nearly 22%, an increase of about $7 to $8 million for the administration to the SNAP program alone.

Furthermore, H.R. 1 now penalizes states for errors by tying the state's payment error rate to share in the cost of the actual SNAP benefits. This has never happened before in the history of the program where the federal government has shifted this type of cost to states. If Virginia's payment error rate for SNAP benefits is at or above 6%, the state pays a portion of the benefits.

Right now, our calculated payment error rate for as of July of 25 was 11.5%. This policy exposure estimates that the cost to the Commonwealth is about $211 million in the first year of the biennium and $270 million in the second year of the biennium. This massive state cost will undoubtedly have downstream effects and consequences for our local budgets and needs in our community.

H.R.1 also eliminates existing exemptions on SNAP-related work requirements, imposing them on highly vulnerable populations. Veterans, the homeless, former foster youth under the age of 24, and families with children under 14 are required to work or to volunteer up to 80 hours per month

in order to maintain their SNAP benefits. They can also participate in education or training. However, if they do not, that will result in a loss of benefits. The work requirements under SNAP are not new to the Department of Social Services.

We've been doing work requirements for decades. However, the sort of removing vulnerable populations is definitely going to show an increase in need. Finally, as it relates to SNAP, most immigrants, including refugees and asylees, are now ineligible for SNAP, forcing them to turn to local community resources after the renewal for their benefits happens next.

As it relates specifically to Medicaid, our workload is going to increase significantly beginning January the 1st of 2027, when the current Medicaid expansion population must undergo eligibility recertification twice a year. In Fairfax, this impacts approximately 50,000 people annually, representing about one-third, slightly under one-third of our active Medicaid population.

This massive surge in workload cannot be absorbed without critical and immediate state investments in modernizing the Virginia case management system. That's the system that we use to process public assistance benefits. Without this update, we face a substantial backlog in timely service to our county residents to access health care services.

Similar to SNAP, H.R. 1 also narrows eligibility for the immigrant population, Which means that people who are currently receiving SNAP benefits are going to be really overwhelmingly sort of without health insurance and needing to access potentially our federally qualified health centers, free clinics, or go without health care.

Finally, while the work requirements and community engagement benefits are not new to the SNAP program, they are new to the Medicaid program. This is a completely new mandate under H.R. 1 in that the local government is responsible, the local Department of Social Services is responsible for monitoring compliance with this work requirement, which represents an unfunded increase in local workload and the administration of the social services programs.
